title: System Design Quiz
description: Check the main idea from each of the 30 lessons. Think about the goal, the data, and what happens when a part fails. Review the explanations and try again.

questions.question: A system design should explain what happens when a needed part fails.
questions.explanation: A plan must cover failures as well as the happy path. Users still need a clear result or error when a part cannot respond.

questions.question: What should a tradeoff note include?
options: Only the chosen tool name
The benefit, the cost, and why the choice fits
A promise that the choice will never change
questions.explanation: A useful note explains what you gain, what you give up, and why the choice fits the current needs. New evidence may change the decision.

questions.question: A search worked but found no matching books. What should the learner see?
options: A clear empty-result message
An endless loading symbol
A message that the whole database is broken
questions.explanation: An empty result is still a successful search. The page should explain that no books matched, so the learner can try different words.

questions.question: Why might a daily average be too small for planning the busiest time?
options: Every minute has exactly the same demand
Many learners may arrive together at lunch
A day never has any quiet minutes
questions.explanation: Demand changes during the day. A lunch rush may produce far more requests per second than the average across several hours.

questions.question: A p95 time of 130 ms means every recorded request finished within 130 ms.
questions.explanation: p95 describes a point near the slow end, not the maximum. In our 20-sample example, one request took 600 ms even though p95 was 130 ms.

questions.question: The search works but no title matches. Which reply fits this contract?
options: 200 OK with an empty items list
404 for the whole search endpoint
200 OK containing a database password
questions.explanation: The collection search succeeded and found zero matches. A private database password must never be part of this public reply.

questions.question: Two different book records may have the same title if they have different stable IDs.
questions.explanation: A title is not guaranteed to be unique. Stable IDs distinguish records even when their titles match or later change.

questions.question: A document database never needs rules about field types or valid values.
questions.explanation: Flexible storage still needs clear data rules. The app or database must validate fields so the rest of the system can use them safely.

questions.question: Creating a normal title index prevents two books from having the same title.
questions.explanation: A normal index can contain repeated values. Preventing duplicates requires a unique constraint or unique index, and titles are often not unique.

questions.question: The loan insert fails after the copy is marked unavailable inside a transaction. What should the caller do?
options: Roll back the transaction
Commit the incomplete changes
Keep the write lock forever
questions.explanation: Rollback cancels the uncommitted copy claim as well. Committing after the failed insert would leave the data half changed.

questions.question: Adding more app servers always removes a database bottleneck.
questions.explanation: The new servers still use the same database. Improve that part or reduce the work sent to it, then measure again.

questions.question: All app servers are unhealthy. What should the balancer do?
options: Choose an array item anyway
Return a clear unavailable result
Pretend the request succeeded
questions.explanation: There is no safe target. A clear error lets the caller decide what to do instead of receiving a false success.

questions.question: A cached item found and reused is a cache ___.
questions.explanation: A hit reuses a usable saved answer. A miss needs another source to supply the answer.

questions.question: Changing a file's contents guarantees every old cached page immediately links to the new file.
questions.explanation: An old page may still point to the old address. Plan freshness for the page and use new file names for changed versions.

questions.question: In the trace, when can the replica still report 2 after the leader has replied saved?
options: During the delay before it applies the update
Never
Only if there are no reads
questions.explanation: The asynchronous leader replied before the replica caught up. That gap is replication lag.

questions.question: Equal record counts on every shard guarantee equal request traffic.
questions.explanation: One shard may hold a very popular key. Measure request work as well as the amount of stored data.

questions.question: A fresh read alone prevents two simultaneous checkout requests from both reserving the same copy.
questions.explanation: Both requests could read available before either writes. The check and reservation must happen under an atomic rule, such as an appropriate transaction.

questions.question: A worker finishes a job, then crashes before sending its acknowledgment. What must the design allow for?
options: The job may be delivered again
The job can never appear again
The queue knows every outside effect automatically
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery can repeat an unacknowledged job. The effect and completion rule must handle that duplicate safely.

questions.question: A timeout proves that the server made no change.
questions.explanation: The server may have completed the change before the reply was lost. Treat the result as uncertain and use a safe retry rule.

questions.question: The state that allows a limited recovery probe is called ___.
questions.explanation: Half-open allows limited test work. Success can close the breaker; failure opens it again under the chosen policy.

questions.question: A separate per-person counter on each of ten servers always enforces one shared limit correctly.
questions.explanation: Each server may allow the full limit on its own. A shared or coordinated rule is needed to enforce one limit across servers.

questions.question: The target for how long a restore should take is called ___ (use the three-letter name).
questions.explanation: RTO means recovery time objective. RPO describes the amount of recent work the recovery plan may lose.

questions.question: Which signal best shows the timed steps of one request through several parts?
options: A trace
A total disk-space number
A list of user passwords
questions.explanation: A trace joins timed steps for one request. Metrics summarize numbers, while logs record individual events.

questions.question: A public book search should collect every reader's home address just in case it is useful later.
questions.explanation: Collect only the facts needed for the job. Unnecessary personal data creates extra privacy risk and extra work to protect it.

questions.question: Borrowing stops whenever the reminder service is slow. What should the design review examine first?
options: Whether borrowing really needs to wait for reminders
Whether all names are short enough
Whether the diagram uses more colors
questions.explanation: Unnecessary waiting creates a failure dependency. A durable queued reminder may let borrowing finish while reminders catch up later.

questions.question: The loan was saved, but the reply was lost. What should a retry with the same request ID do?
options: Create a second loan
Return the saved result after checking the same request details
Erase every loan
questions.explanation: A durable request result lets a safe retry return the original outcome. Reusing the ID for different details must be rejected.

questions.question: A hard-to-guess short link is enough to protect a private document from anyone who receives that link.
questions.explanation: A short code is a lookup label. Private content still needs permission checks at the service that returns it.

questions.question: A reader reconnects after seeing sequence 12. What should catch-up request?
options: Only messages currently in server memory
Saved permitted messages after sequence 12
Every private group in the school
questions.explanation: Saved history and a sequence cursor let a member catch up in order. Membership must still be checked before returning messages.

questions.question: A cached feed contains an old private post ID. Before returning its text, what should happen?
options: Return it because the ID is cached
Check the reader's current permission
Make every post public
questions.explanation: Cached IDs do not grant permission. Current visibility, deletion, and access rules must still protect the post.

questions.question: Why use an immutable final key or an exact stored version after scanning?
options: To serve the same bytes that passed the checks
To make all files public
To remove the need for permission checks
questions.explanation: A later overwrite must not replace checked bytes with unchecked content. Permission checks are still needed for downloads.
